paras: The threatened lynching of Si Bearden took place at Springfield, Missouri, in August and September 1888, when mobs surrounded the Springfield jail and threatened to lynch Bearden, a Black man accused of shooting police officer Palmer. Bearden, badly wounded by officers at his capture, was not lynched; after a second mob gathered, Sheriff Dodson moved him to the St. Louis jail for safe keeping. Wire reports of the mob of 300 ran in papers across the country.

According to the wire reports, Bearden shot Officer Palmer on Wednesday, August 8, 1888. A Dakota digest said the officer was shot by a man he was attempting to arrest. The first dispatch called Palmer 'fatally wounded', while a Springfield dispatch of August 11 said he was 'dangerously wounded'.

Officers found Bearden on a farm about six miles east of Springfield on the morning of August 10. According to the Springfield dispatch, he drew a revolver when asked to surrender, and Officer Snow shot him through the body before he could fire. A St. Louis Post-Dispatch special said instead that he was taken only after 'his body had been filled with lead'.

He was placed in the Springfield jail, which the Post-Dispatch special said was soon surrounded by a mob of 300 men threatening to lynch him. A Wilmington summary put the crowd at 'several hundred men', and an Oregon weekly described them as 'armed men'. Reports agreed that he was so badly wounded that he was expected to die, and the Indianapolis Journal wrote that he would likely 'die without hanging'.

Bearden survived his wounds. A St. Louis dispatch of September 11 reported that a mob had surrounded the Springfield jail 'the other night' and that he 'had such a narrow escape from Judge Lynch' that Sheriff Dodson decided to move him.

Bearden was brought to St. Louis on the night of September 10 and lodged in jail for safe keeping. The September dispatch described him as the man 'who murdered Officer Palmore', but no report of Palmer's death appears in the coverage. No report of an arrest of mob members, or of Bearden's trial, was found.

The episode reached the press through two August wires and one September wire, mostly as short items in news digests. The Post-Dispatch special ran on August 11 in Washington, Richmond, St. Paul, Indianapolis and Savannah, and was reprinted over the following week in Atlanta and in weeklies in Nebraska and Oregon. The separate Springfield dispatch of August 11, which named Officer Snow and mentioned no mob, appeared in Kansas and Indian Territory weeklies.

Headlines named the accused by race and treated him as a criminal: the Richmond Dispatch used 'A Negro Desperado Shot', the St. Paul Daily Globe called his body 'The Carcass of a Negro Murderer Perforated with Bullets', and the Savannah Morning News ran 'Bullets in a Brute's Body. An Angry Mob Anxious to Hang Him Despite His Wounds'. The McCook Tribune printed the item with the lynching of Amos Miller in Tennessee under one headline, 'Dealt With by Judge Lynch', although Bearden had not been lynched. None of the August items commented on the mob, which was reported only as a threat.

The September wire framed the transfer as a near miss, under heads such as 'Nearly Had Him' in San Antonio and 'Narrowly Escaped Lynching' in Memphis. It was also carried in German by Baltimore's Der Deutsche Correspondent and, on September 20, by the Chariton Courier in Missouri.

The papers differed on the date of the shooting: most said Wednesday, while the Wilmington Daily Republican said Thursday. They also differed on Palmer's condition, from 'dangerously wounded' to 'fatally wounded' to 'murdered'. The accused's name was printed in at least eight forms, from Bearden and Reardon to S. J. Berdon and Si Beardon.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Si Bearden
bases: A mob of about 300 surrounded the Springfield jail threatening to lynch a wounded Black prisoner accused of shooting a policeman (A2, A3), and a later mob at the jail led the sheriff to move him to St. Louis (A19, A20); no killing is reported.

The mob threatened to lynch Bearden for the shooting of Officer Palmer (A2, A3), but no paper reports that he was killed; he was last reported alive in the St. Louis jail (A19, A20), so this was a threatened or attempted lynching, not a completed one.

The Post-Dispatch wire (A3) and the differently worded Wilmington summary (A5) agree on the capture and the mob at the jail, and a separate September wire (A19, A20) confirms a mob at the Springfield jail and the prisoner's removal.

accounts.label: Post-Dispatch special (wire, Aug. 10)
accounts.gist: Bearden was captured with his body 'filled with lead' and jailed; a mob of 300 surrounded the jail threatening to lynch him, though he was expected to die of his wounds.

accounts.label: Springfield dispatch of Aug. 11 (wire)
accounts.gist: Officers surrounded Berdon on a farm six miles east; he drew a revolver when told to surrender and Officer Snow shot him; he lay in jail in critical condition. It mentions no mob.

accounts.label: St. Louis dispatch of Sept. 11 (wire)
accounts.gist: After a mob surrounded the Springfield jail 'the other night', Sheriff Dodson brought Beardon to St. Louis for safe keeping.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Post-Dispatch special verbatim as a brief, calling the accused 'the desperado' and reporting the mob without comment.
Some headlines dehumanized the prisoner ('Bullets in a Brute's Body', 'The Carcass of a Negro Murderer Perforated with Bullets') while reporting the mob's threat as news.
The September wire framed the episode as a near-lynching ('Nearly Had Him', 'Narrowly Escaped Lynching') and the removal as safe keeping.

conflicts.note: The Post-Dispatch wire and the September dispatch agree on Wednesday, August 8.
No report of Palmer's death appears in the coverage; the September wire's 'murdered' implies he died.
All refer to the same man; the Springfield and September dispatches agree on a name close to Beardon.
